title: [Vantage Point] Semirara: The government is auctioning an energy crisis
summary: The government’s pursuit of the highest financial offer may inadvertently trigger the Philippines' most expensive energy failure

blocks.text: As the government prepares to auction the Semirara coal mine to the highest bidder, its focus on maximizing state revenues over technical competence threatens to trigger a national energy crisis. With the Acacia pit rapidly flooding with seawater and production targets drastically slashed, handing the operation to a new contractor unprepared for this severe engineering failure risks forcing electricity consumers, displaced workers, and the local economy to absorb the catastrophic cost of regulatory negligence.

The Philippine government unequivocally possesses the right to demand a superior return from the vast coal reserves of Semirara Island. These vital natural resources belong fundamentally to the state, not to the incumbent operator, Semirara Mining and Power Corp. (SMPC). It is thus prudent for regulators to reassess the terms as Coal Operating Contract No. 5 approaches its July 14, 2027, expiration.

However, in its eagerness to maximize state revenues, the Department of Energy (DOE) appears to be losing sight of a crucial engineering reality: an auction is only as valuable as the asset that can be operated.

If the winning bidder cannot immediately master a rapidly flooding pit, mobilize highly specialized equipment, retain a massive workforce, and continuously produce coal, the government’s pursuit of the highest financial offer will inadvertently trigger the nation’s most expensive energy failure.
The rapidly deteriorating physical condition of the mine makes the demand for absolute transparency not just urgent, but critical to our national energy security.

SMPC has disclosed that seawater is currently surging into the Acacia mine at an astonishing rate of approximately 30,000 cubic meters an hour. To put this catastrophic volume into perspective, it is equivalent to 12 Olympic-size swimming pools flooding the active mining site every single hour—a deluge that now vastly exceeds the mine’s existing pumping capacity.

The structural integrity of the site is already failing under this pressure. On September 20, dumped and in-situ material from North Block 1 Dam 2 completely collapsed, dangerously redirecting surface runoff directly toward the pit.
Consequently, crucial stripping operations in Acacia have been indefinitely suspended while SMPC scrambles to construct another cut-off wall and undertakes emergency remedial work.

This structural failure is profoundly alarming because the Acacia pit had been heavily relied upon to supply the vast majority of the company’s projected coal production in 2027. Are regulators preparing to hand over a lucrative natural resource, or are they blindly auctioning a poisoned chalice?

The human and production consequences resulting from this operational crisis are already highly measurable and accelerating. Initially, SMPC announced sudden redundancies affecting 462 mine-site employees, but the situation quickly worsened, leading the company to add another 996 workers to the chopping block, bringing the total to a staggering 1,458 displaced individuals.

Furthermore, its revised 2026 production target has been slashed to just 12 million metric tons, representing a precipitous drop of nearly 40% below the record 19.9 million tons the company produced in 2025.

SMPC claims that lingering uncertainty over the upcoming contract severely complicates any further investments in the massive pumps, power systems, and supporting infrastructure required to save the pit.

While that explanation is financially plausible from a corporate standpoint, it does not absolve SMPC of its underlying responsibility to explain exactly how the mine was allowed to reach this precarious, flooded condition under its watch, nor does it clarify how much the required remediation will ultimately cost the next operator.

The collateral economic damage is swiftly moving far beyond the company’s immediate payroll. It was reported than on October 11, Island entrepreneur Janice Lim had already experienced slower sales, fewer customers, and delayed payments as workers grew increasingly terrified about their immediate job security.

At the Divine Word School of Semirara Island, where SMPC historically provides approximately P90 million annually for free tuition and the education of employees’ children, more than 1,500 students now face a completely uncertain future, according to the student-government president.

These accounts make one point unmistakable: a credible transition plan crafted by the government must robustly protect households, schools, and small businesses, rather than merely keeping a lucrative mine permit alive on paper.

This brings us to the glaring issue of regulatory negligence. The DOE prudently terminated the earlier bid round in September following the initial seawater problem, ongoing legal disputes, and mounting stakeholder concerns, stating that a new auction would seek greater government revenue, domestic coal commitments, and enhanced consumer benefits. But restarting this complex process in November or December leaves barely seven months before the contract’s expiry.

A new operator would have to seamlessly arrange billions in financing, secure specialized equipment, recruit and train thousands of workers, master a highly complex mine plan, and assume control of a pit that is actively sinking.

The governance problem surrounding this transition is becoming significantly harder to defend. SMPC states that the regulatory process has produced no bid bulletins, no prequalification screening, no model contract, and no official answers to its vital technical questions—even as the highest financial offer, rather than demonstrated mining competence and engineering capability, remains the sole determinant of the winner.

When more than P55 billion in existing mine investments, thousands of local jobs, and critical domestic coal production are exposed to this level of uncertainty, procedural silence from the DOE morphs into a severe public-interest risk.

This dispute is further complicated by a contentious court case over the heavy equipment and infrastructure already situated on Semirara Island. SMPC filed a petition for declaratory relief after the DOE demanded a full inventory of its property, plant, and equipment, stating this proprietary information would be made available to competing bidders.

blocks.caption: Semirara takes DOE data dispute to court amid race for biggest coal mine

blocks.text: The DOE maintains that assets whose costs have been recovered—and materials not removed within one year after contract termination—may vest in the government and be made available to the eventual winner. SMPC firmly argues that cost recovery is merely reimbursement, not a transfer of ownership, and relies on Presidential Decree 972 to preserve its absolute title and removal rights.

SMPC highlights that it paid an impressive P43.4 billion in government share and P3.7 billion in taxes from 2021 through the first half of 2026. Those figures should absolutely be independently verified, but the company’s shutdown warnings should not simply frighten the government into granting a perpetual, automatic extension.

The government has no mandate to unconditionally preserve SMPC’s incumbency. It must, however, prove that replacing the operator—or retaining it through a genuinely competitive bidding process—will successfully protect the grid, public revenues, and operating continuity.

An incumbent’s experience creates a natural advantage, not a permanent entitlement. But neither should the government confuse a large financial bid with the actual technical ability to operate an unusually difficult, failing mine.
The public-interest solution is to make the competition truly real and grounded in engineering reality.

The DOE must comprehensively disclose the scoring system, require minimum experience, verify committed technical personnel, and explicitly outline the financial consequences if the winner fails to keep the water out.

Until these fundamental questions are fully answered, the government is not simply auctioning coal; it is auctioning an impending energy cost shock and unfairly forcing electricity consumers to absorb the catastrophic risk. – Rappler.com
